source_refs.note: Chapter 25 exercise (PDF 143-144) solved: 10 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 10 short, 2 constructed response and 5 descriptive questions (retrosynthetic trees, syntheses and conversions as equations). Book corrections: MCQ II, VII, X.

blocks.prompt: I) After disconnection the components obtained are called:
blocks.explanation: A disconnection breaks the target molecule into fragments called synthons (25.1.2). Synthetic equivalents are the real reagents that do the job of the synthons.

blocks.prompt: II) How will you convert the amide functional group (-C≡N) to the amine group?
blocks.explanation: –C≡N is reduced to the amine; e.g. LiAlH₄ adds hydrogen: R–C≡N → (LiAlH₄) R–CH₂–NH₂ (beyond the chapter). The amide group –CONH₂ is also changed into the amine by reduction with LiAlH₄ (Figure 25.3). Either way it is a reduction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The question calls –C≡N 'the amide functional group'. –C≡N is the nitrile (cyano) group; the amide group is –CONH₂. Both are turned into an amine by reduction, so the answer (b) stands.

blocks.prompt: III) What does this arrow (⟹) mean in organic chemistry reactions?
blocks.explanation: The open-ended arrow ⇒ is the retrosynthetic arrow: it is read 'is made from' and points from the target molecule back to simpler starting materials (25.1.2).

blocks.prompt: IV) Which reagent you will choose to convert aldehyde group into alcohol?
blocks.explanation:
An aldehyde is reduced to a primary alcohol by NaBH₄ followed by acid work-up (Figure 25.3):
CH₃CHO → (NaBH₄/H₃O⁺) CH₃CH₂OH
KMnO₄/H⁺ is an oxidising agent.

blocks.prompt: V) Which reagent is commonly used to oxidize primary alcohol into carboxylic acid?
blocks.explanation:
Acidified potassium dichromate oxidises a primary alcohol to the aldehyde and then to the carboxylic acid (Figure 25.3):
CH₃CH₂OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇, H₂SO₄) CH₃COOH
H₂/Pd, LiAlH₄ and NaBH₄ are reducing agents.

blocks.prompt: VI) When toluene is treated with KMnO₄/H₂SO₄, we obtain:
blocks.explanation:
Acidified KMnO₄ oxidises the CH₃ side chain of toluene to –COOH (Figure 25.4):
C₆H₅CH₃ → (KMnO₄/H₂SO₄) C₆H₅COOH (benzoic acid)

blocks.prompt: VII) Which functional group is formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol in the presence of an acid as catalyst?
blocks.explanation:
Esterification (25.2.1):
CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → (H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O
The product is an ester.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (c) is printed 'aldehdye'; it should read aldehyde.

blocks.prompt:
VIII) What is compound A in the given sequence?
phenol → (nitration) nitrophenol → (reduction) aminophenol → (acetylation) A
blocks.explanation:
This is the synthesis of paracetamol (25.3.1):
phenol → (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) 4-nitrophenol → (Sn + HCl) 4-aminophenol → (CH₃COCl) paracetamol
Acetylation puts CH₃CO– on the –NH₂ group, giving HO–C₆H₄–NHCOCH₃.

blocks.prompt: IX) In organic synthesis, what is the primary purpose of a 'Functional Group Interconversion' (FGI)?

options.text: To break the molecule into smaller fragments
To increase total number of carbon atoms in molecule
To make the molecule more reactive
To change the functional group into another to enable a specific reaction

blocks.explanation: FGI is the conversion of one functional group into another to reach the target molecule, e.g. –NH₂ ⇒ –NO₂ in the retrosynthesis of aniline, because a nitro group is easy to put on benzene (25.1.2, 25.2.2).

blocks.prompt: X) The drug 'Halicin' developed by AI work as an:
blocks.explanation: Halicin was picked out by a machine-learning model as a molecule with antibacterial properties; it killed many disease-causing bacteria that were resistant to treatment (25.4). So it works as an antibiotic.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (a) is printed 'antiviral drung'; it should read antiviral drug. 'work as an' should read 'works as an'.

blocks.prompt: a) Differentiate between synthesis and retrosynthesis.
blocks.explanation: Retrosynthesis is exactly the opposite of synthesis: it plans the route on paper, and synthesis then follows it.

rows: Target molecule is prepared from simple, commercially available starting materials
Target molecule is broken down into simpler, readily available starting materials
Works forward: starting material → target molecule
Works backward: target molecule ⇒ starting material
Uses real reactions, reagents and conditions (arrow →)
Uses imaginary disconnections and FGI (open arrow ⇒)

blocks.prompt: b) How a carboxylic group is converted to an amide group?
blocks.explanation:
The acid is first changed into its acid chloride with SOCl₂, which then reacts with ammonia (Figure 25.3):
CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + SO₂ + HCl
CH₃COCl + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + HCl
(Figure 25.3 also shows the acid reacting with NH₃ directly.)

blocks.prompt: c) How synthon and synthetic equivalent are related to each other?
blocks.explanation:
A synthon is a fragment (usually an ion) obtained by disconnecting the target molecule; it is usually unstable and cannot be used itself. Its synthetic equivalent is the real, stable reagent that carries out the function of that synthon.
e.g. C₆H₅⁻ ≡ benzene, NO₂⁺ ≡ HNO₃, CH₃CO⁺ ≡ CH₃COCl.

blocks.prompt: d) Write down the formula of the reagent used for oxidation of organic compounds.
blocks.explanation:
Acidified potassium dichromate, K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ (e.g. alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid).
Acidified potassium permanganate, KMnO₄/H₂SO₄, is also used (e.g. toluene → benzoic acid) (Figures 25.3, 25.4).

blocks.prompt: e) Show with equations how alcohol can be converted into amines, alkenes and halogenoalkanes.
blocks.explanation:
Halogenoalkane: CH₃CH₂OH → (PBr₃) CH₃CH₂Br (or R–CH₂–OH + SOCl₂ → R–CH₂–Cl + SO₂ + HCl)
Alkene: CH₃CH₂OH → (conc. H₂SO₄, heat) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
Amine (through the halogenoalkane): CH₃CH₂Br + NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + HBr (Figure 25.3, 25.1.1)

blocks.prompt: f) What is a disconnection in retrosynthesis of a molecule?
blocks.explanation:
Disconnection is the imaginary breaking of a bond of the target molecule into simpler fragments (synthons). The bond is chosen so that it gives a big structural simplification; it is shown by a wavy line across the bond and the arrow ⇒.
e.g. ethyl acetate disconnected at the C(=O)–O bond gives CH₃CO⁺ and C₂H₅O⁻.

blocks.prompt: g) Mention one useful application of FGI in organic synthesis?
blocks.explanation: FGI lets a group that is hard to introduce be made from one that is easy to introduce. e.g. –NH₂ cannot easily be put on benzene, so aniline ⇒ (FGI) nitrobenzene: benzene is nitrated (easy electrophilic substitution) and the –NO₂ is then reduced with Sn/HCl to –NH₂ (25.2.2).

blocks.prompt: h) Give one method for the reduction of a nitro group (-NO₂) to an amino group (-NH₂).
blocks.explanation:
Reduction with tin and hydrochloric acid (Sn + HCl):
C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → (Sn/HCl) C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O (nitrobenzene → aniline, Figure 25.4)

blocks.prompt: i) How a carboxylic group is converted to an alcohol?
blocks.explanation:
By reduction with lithium aluminium hydride, LiAlH₄ (Figure 25.3):
CH₃COOH + 4[H] → (LiAlH₄) CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O

blocks.prompt: j) Design synthesis of 3-chloronitrobenzene and 2-chloronitrobenzene starting from benzene in two steps.
blocks.explanation:
The order of steps depends on the directing effect of the first group (Chapter 20, 20.4).
3-Chloronitrobenzene: nitrate first, then chlorinate; –NO₂ is meta-directing.
C₆H₆ → (conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄) C₆H₅NO₂ → (Cl₂/FeCl₃) 3-ClC₆H₄NO₂
2-Chloronitrobenzene: chlorinate first, then nitrate; –Cl is ortho/para-directing.
C₆H₆ → (Cl₂/FeCl₃) C₆H₅Cl → (conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄) 2-ClC₆H₄NO₂ (+ 4-isomer, separated)

blocks.prompt: a) Construct the functional group interconversion flow sheet and highlight the important reagents and conversions involved.
blocks.explanation:
Aliphatic flow sheet (Figure 25.3), two-carbon compounds:
• Alkene ⇄ halogenoalkane: CH₂=CH₂ → (HBr) CH₃CH₂Br; CH₃CH₂Br → (KOH, alcoholic) CH₂=CH₂
• Alkene ⇄ alcohol: CH₂=CH₂ → (H₂O, H₂SO₄) CH₃CH₂OH; CH₃CH₂OH → (heat, H₂SO₄) CH₂=CH₂
• Alcohol ⇄ halogenoalkane: CH₃CH₂OH → (PBr₃) CH₃CH₂Br; CH₃CH₂Br → (KOH, aq) CH₃CH₂OH
• Halogenoalkane/alcohol → amine: CH₃CH₂Br → (NH₃) CH₃CH₂NH₂
• Alcohol ⇄ aldehyde: CH₃CH₂OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇, H₂SO₄) CH₃CHO; CH₃CHO → (NaBH₄) CH₃CH₂OH
• Aldehyde → carboxylic acid: CH₃CHO → (V₂O₅, air) CH₃COOH
• Alcohol ⇄ carboxylic acid: CH₃CH₂OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇, H₂SO₄) CH₃COOH; CH₃COOH → (LiAlH₄) CH₃CH₂OH
• Carboxylic acid → ester: CH₃COOH → (C₂H₅OH, H⁺) CH₃COOC₂H₅
• Carboxylic acid → acid halide: CH₃COOH → (SOCl₂) CH₃COCl
• Acid or acid halide → amide: → (NH₃) CH₃CONH₂; amide → (LiAlH₄) CH₃CH₂NH₂
Aromatic flow sheet (Figure 25.4), from benzene:
• → (CH₃Cl/AlCl₃) toluene → (KMnO₄/H₂SO₄) benzoic acid; toluene → (i) Cl₂, light (ii) KOH(aq) benzyl alcohol
• → (SO₃/H₂SO₄) benzene sulfonic acid → (i) NaOH (ii) HCl phenol
• → (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) nitrobenzene → (Sn, HCl) aniline
• → (CH₃COCl/AlCl₃) acetophenone
Important reagents: oxidising agents K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄ and KMnO₄/H₂SO₄; reducing agents NaBH₄, LiAlH₄ and Sn/HCl; KOH (aqueous for substitution, alcoholic for elimination); PBr₃ and SOCl₂ for –OH → halide; H₂SO₄ as catalyst or dehydrating agent; AlCl₃ for Friedel-Crafts reactions.

blocks.prompt: b) Construct the retrosynthetic tree for the paracetamol and then design its synthesis.
blocks.explanation:
Paracetamol (TM) = HO–C₆H₄–NHCOCH₃ (4-hydroxy on the ring, para to the amide group) (25.3.1).
Retrosynthetic tree:
Step I Disconnection: break the amide C–N bond: TM ⇒ HO–C₆H₄–NH⁻ (synthon A) + CH₃CO⁺ (synthon B)
Step II Synthetic equivalents: synthon A ≡ 4-aminophenol; synthon B ≡ acyl chloride CH₃COCl (they react by nucleophilic addition-elimination)
Step III FGI: 4-aminophenol ⇒ 4-nitrophenol (4-nitrophenol is easy to prepare and is reduced to 4-aminophenol)
Step IV Disconnection: break the C–NO₂ bond of 4-nitrophenol: ⇒ HO–C₆H₄⁻ (synthon A) + NO₂⁺ (synthon B)
Step V Synthetic equivalents: HO–C₆H₄⁻ ≡ phenol; NO₂⁺ ≡ nitric acid HNO₃ (starting materials)
Synthesis:
C₆H₅OH → (HNO₃/H₂SO₄) HO–C₆H₄–NO₂ (4-nitrophenol)
HO–C₆H₄–NO₂ → (Sn + HCl) HO–C₆H₄–NH₂ (4-aminophenol)
HO–C₆H₄–NH₂ + CH₃COCl → HO–C₆H₄–NHCOCH₃ (paracetamol) + HCl

blocks.prompt: Q4. Give a detailed account of importance of retrosynthesis in organic synthesis.
blocks.explanation:
Retrosynthesis plans a synthesis backwards, from the target molecule (TM) to simple starting materials. Its importance:
1. It breaks a complex TM, by a series of disconnections, into simple, cheap and easily available starting materials; complex structures then look simple and achievable (25.3).
2. It identifies which bonds to break (those giving the greatest structural simplification) and gives the synthons and their synthetic equivalents, i.e. the actual reagents to use.
3. It shows where FGI is needed, e.g. aniline ⇒ nitrobenzene, because a nitro group is easy to introduce and then reduce (25.2.2).
4. The retrosynthetic tree shows all possible disconnections and routes, so the best route can be chosen: the least number of steps and the highest overall yield (25.1).
5. It decodes the 'series of steps' of a direct synthesis, e.g. phenol → paracetamol (nitration, reduction, acetylation) and phenol → aspirin (carboxylation, acetylation) (25.3).
6. It is the main tool for designing pharmaceutical products, and it made landmark syntheses possible, e.g. cholesterol (early 1950s) and vitamin B₁₂ (1972, over 100 steps).
Example: ethyl acetate ⇒ (disconnect C(=O)–O) CH₃CO⁺ + C₂H₅O⁻ ≡ acetic acid + ethanol; synthesis: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → (H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

blocks.prompt: Q5. Explain the role of halogenoalkanes in retrosynthesis of organic molecules.
blocks.explanation:
Halogenoalkanes are key intermediates (a 'hub') in retrosynthesis because the C–X bond is easily made and easily replaced:
1. Synthetic equivalents of carbocation synthons: when a C–N, C–O or C–C bond is disconnected, the alkyl part is often the cation R⁺, and its synthetic equivalent is the halogenoalkane R–X. e.g. R–CH₂–NH₂ ⇒ R–CH₂⁺ + NH₂⁻ ≡ R–CH₂–Cl + NH₃:
R–CH₂–Cl + NH₃ → R–CH₂–NH₂ + HCl (25.1.1)
2. Made by FGI from alcohols, which are easily available: R–CH₂–OH → (SOCl₂) R–CH₂–Cl; CH₃CH₂OH → (PBr₃) CH₃CH₂Br. So the amine synthesis is planned as alcohol → halogenoalkane → amine.
3. Converted into many other groups (Figure 25.3):
CH₃CH₂Br → (KOH, aq) CH₃CH₂OH (substitution)
CH₃CH₂Br → (KOH, alcoholic) CH₂=CH₂ (elimination)
CH₃CH₂Br → (NH₃) CH₃CH₂NH₂
and alkenes give halogenoalkanes: CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br.
4. C–C bond formation on benzene: CH₃Cl is the synthetic equivalent of CH₃⁺ in Friedel-Crafts alkylation: C₆H₆ + CH₃Cl → (AlCl₃) C₆H₅CH₃ + HCl (Figure 25.4).
5. Side-chain halogenation gives a route to benzyl alcohol: C₆H₅CH₃ → (Cl₂, light) C₆H₅CH₂Cl → (KOH, aq) C₆H₅CH₂OH.
Thus halogenoalkanes link alcohols, alkenes, amines and aromatic compounds in a retrosynthetic plan.

blocks.prompt: Q6. Construct the retrosynthetic tree for the aspirin and then design its synthesis.
blocks.explanation:
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, TM): a benzene ring with –COOH and, on the neighbouring carbon, –O–CO–CH₃ (25.3.2).
Retrosynthetic tree:
Step I Disconnection-I: break the C–O bond of the ester link: TM ⇒ 2-carboxyphenoxide ion ⁻O–C₆H₄–COOH (synthon A) + CH₃CO⁺ (synthon B)
Step II Synthetic equivalents: synthon A ≡ salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid, HO–C₆H₄–COOH); synthon B ≡ acetic anhydride (CH₃CO)₂O
Step III Disconnection-II: break the ring C–COOH bond of salicylic acid: ⇒ ring carbanion next to OH (synthon A) + ⁺COOH (synthon B)
Step IV Synthetic equivalents: phenol (C₆H₅OH) and carbon dioxide (O=C=O)
Synthesis:
C₆H₅OH → ((i) CO₂, high T and P (ii) H₂SO₄) HO–C₆H₄–COOH (salicylic acid)
HO–C₆H₄–COOH + (CH₃CO)₂O → (H₃PO₄, heat) CH₃COO–C₆H₄–COOH (aspirin) + CH₃COOH
So aspirin is made from phenol in two steps: carboxylation, then acetylation (esterification of the –OH).

blocks.prompt:
Q7. Design the synthesis of the following molecules starting from benzene.
a) aniline (benzene ring with –NH₂) b) toluene (benzene ring with –CH₃) c) benzoic acid (benzene ring with –COOH) d) benzyl alcohol (benzene ring with –CH₂-OH)
blocks.explanation:
All four start from benzene (Figure 25.4):
a) Aniline (C₆H₅NH₂): nitration, then reduction
C₆H₆ → (conc. HNO₃/conc. H₂SO₄) C₆H₅NO₂ → (Sn + HCl) C₆H₅NH₂
b) Toluene (C₆H₅CH₃): Friedel-Crafts alkylation
C₆H₆ + CH₃Cl → (AlCl₃) C₆H₅CH₃ + HCl
c) Benzoic acid (C₆H₅COOH): make toluene as in (b), then oxidise the side chain
C₆H₆ → (CH₃Cl/AlCl₃) C₆H₅CH₃ → (KMnO₄/H₂SO₄) C₆H₅COOH
d) Benzyl alcohol (C₆H₅CH₂OH): make toluene, chlorinate the side chain in light, then hydrolyse with aqueous KOH
C₆H₆ → (CH₃Cl/AlCl₃) C₆H₅CH₃ → (Cl₂, light) C₆H₅CH₂Cl → (KOH, aq) C₆H₅CH₂OH + KCl

blocks.prompt:
Q8. How will you carry out the following conversions?
a) CH₃—CH₃ → CH₃—COOH
b) CH₂=CH₂ → CH₃—CH₂—OH
c) CH₃—CH₂—CH₂—Cl → CH₃—CH=CH₂
d) CH₃—COOH → CH₃—CH₂—OH
blocks.explanation:
a) Ethane → acetic acid: chlorinate (free radical substitution in UV light, Class XI), hydrolyse, then oxidise
CH₃–CH₃ + Cl₂ → (UV light) CH₃CH₂Cl + HCl
CH₃CH₂Cl + KOH(aq) → CH₃CH₂OH + KCl
CH₃CH₂OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇, H₂SO₄) CH₃COOH
b) Ethene → ethanol: acid-catalysed hydration (Figure 25.3)
CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → (H₂SO₄) CH₃–CH₂–OH
c) 1-Chloropropane → propene: elimination of HCl with alcoholic KOH
CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–Cl + KOH(alcoholic) → (heat) CH₃–CH=CH₂ + KCl + H₂O
d) Acetic acid → ethanol: reduction with LiAlH₄ (Figure 25.3)
CH₃–COOH + 4[H] → (LiAlH₄) CH₃–CH₂–OH + H₂O
